summary: Describes a framework for IPFIX Mediation, defining Mediator components that sit between exporters and collectors of IP flow data. It extends the reference model of RFC 5470 and is informational.

eli5.summary: A middleman that tidies up reports on network traffic before passing them on.

subtitle: A framework for a middleman that sits between IPFIX exporters and collectors and reshapes flow data on the way through.

tldr.problem: The plain Exporter-to-Collector IPFIX architecture can run into scalability problems and lacks the flexibility many measurement applications need.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an IPFIX Mediator that hosts one or more Intermediate Processes (conversion, selection, aggregation, anonymization, correlation) between Collecting and Exporting Processes.
tldr.outcome: The document gives the reference model, the functional blocks, ways to combine them, header-encoding notes and security rules for mediators. It is informational and updates RFC 5470.

today: RFC 6183 is an Informational RFC published in April 2011 that updates RFC 5470, and it has not been obsoleted. It describes a framework, not a protocol, so it does not define new messages.

sections.title: Why a Mediator Is Needed
sections.content:
The IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) architecture of RFC 5470 has IPFIX Devices and IPFIX Collectors talking through the IPFIX protocol. Because IP traffic keeps growing in varied networks, this Exporter-to-Collector design can run into scalability problems, and it does not give the flexibility many measurement applications need. RFC 5982 describes these problems in detail.

The answer is an intermediate entity between Exporters and Collectors. On the data side it may aggregate, correlate, filter and modify Flow Records and Packet Sampling (PSAMP) Packet Reports, saving measurement resources and preprocessing for the Collector. On the protocol side it may convert other formats into IPFIX, or convert IPFIX transport protocols, for example from UDP to the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP), to make export more reliable.

RFC 6183 generalizes this idea as IPFIX Mediation and describes its high-level architecture, key components and characteristics.
sections.eli5: If every router mailed its reports straight to one office, the office would drown in mail. A helper in the middle can sort and shrink the pile first.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
IPFIX Mediation is the manipulation and conversion of a record stream for later export using the IPFIX protocol. A record stream is a stream of records carrying flow-based or packet-based information, in IPFIX Data Records or any other format. The Original Exporter is the IPFIX Device that hosts the Observation Points where packets are actually metered.

An Intermediate Process takes a record stream from Collecting Processes, Metering Processes, IPFIX File Readers, other Intermediate Processes or other sources. It transforms the stream using each record's content, state kept across records, or other data, and passes the result to Exporting Processes, IPFIX File Writers or other Intermediate Processes. It usually runs inside an IPFIX Mediator, though an Original Exporter may host one too.

An IPFIX Mediator is an IPFIX Device that receives a record stream, hosts one or more Intermediate Processes, and exports the result as IPFIX Messages through an Exporting Process. Usually its input comes from a Collecting Process, but it may also come from non-IPFIX sources, for example NetFlow V9 (RFC 3954). The RFC calls the Mediator a generalization of the concentrator and proxy elements in the IPFIX requirements, RFC 3917.
sections.eli5: A mediator is the middleman. Inside it, little workers called Intermediate Processes each do one job on the reports, like merging, filtering or translating.

sections.title: The Mediation Reference Model
sections.content:
The reference model extends the IPFIX model of RFC 5470. An IPFIX Mediator can receive IPFIX Flow Records or PSAMP Packet Reports from other Mediators, Flow Records from IPFIX Original Exporters, Packet Reports from PSAMP Original Exporters, or a record stream from other sources. It then exports Flow Records and Packet Reports to one or more Collectors or to further Mediators, so Mediators can be chained.

The basic Mediator contains one or more Intermediate Processes and one or more Exporting Processes. It normally also has a Collecting Process, and may have several. For non-IPFIX input such as NetFlow, a Mediator needs no Collecting Process and instead takes the record stream directly. The RFC makes no assumption about how a record stream reaches the Mediator.

An Original Exporter can also provide mediation by hosting Intermediate Processes between its Metering and Exporting Processes. An Intermediate Process may likewise sit beside an IPFIX File Reader or Writer, to work on stored records.

A Mediator's Collecting and Exporting Processes are the same as those in RFC 5101, with a few extra duties. The Collecting Process may duplicate its records to several components in sequence or in parallel. The Exporting Process may be told to send Template Withdrawal Messages when templates become invalid, for example after an incoming session failure, and may export the origin of the data (Observation Point, Observation Domain ID, Original Exporter IP address) as extra fields.
sections.eli5: The mediator has an inbox, some workers, and an outbox. Reports come in, get handled by the workers, and go out to the next office, which might be another mediator.

sections.title: What Intermediate Processes Do
sections.content:
All Intermediate Processes may generate a new record stream with context information, report statistics about the upstream Metering and Exporting Processes, keep configurable links between inputs and outputs, and keep statistics on themselves. The RFC names five specific types and says the list is not exhaustive.

  • Conversion: turns non-IPFIX records into IPFIX (for instance mapping NetFlow V9 fields to the IPFIX Information Model), or converts the transport, for example UDP to SCTP, relaying Templates and tracking sessions and Template IDs.
  • Selection: keeps only the records whose chosen field equals a configured value or lies in a configured range. It works like PSAMP selection but on records instead of packets.
  • Aggregation: merges records within a time period, summing counters. Spatial composition merges records that share properties, such as a smaller set of Flow Keys. Temporal composition merges records with identical Flow Keys from the same Observation Point into one longer Flow.
  • Anonymization: deletes fields (for example next-hop addresses, to hide topology) or changes field values (for example IP addresses) according to a privacy policy.
  • Correlation: a special case of aggregation that derives new information, such as one-way delay from pairs of Packet Reports, bidirectional flows from unidirectional ones (RFC 5103), or BGP and VPN details added from other data.

Aggregation and correlation keep caches of records, so they need expiration rules. Cached records expire after a configurable time with no new input, may expire early under resource pressure, and long-running Flows should expire regularly. When the data layout changes, the flowKeyIndicator must be changed to match.
sections.eli5: The workers each have one trick: translate, pick out some reports, add several together, black out secret details, or work out something new by comparing reports.

sections.title: Combining Processes and Message Headers
sections.content:
A Mediator can run several Intermediate Processes at once. In parallel setups each process gets a copy of the whole record stream. In serial setups the output of one process feeds the next. Combining components gives useful tricks: Selection plus Exporting sends records to different Collectors by customer or peering AS number; Selection plus Aggregation shrinks data by aggregating only Flows with few packets, for instance those with 5 packets or fewer; and Anonymization before an IPFIX File Writer removes problem fields before storage.

The RFC also gives header advice for relayed messages. The Export Time can be kept from the incoming session or set to when the message leaves the Mediator, in which case delta timestamp fields must be handled. The Sequence Number on an outgoing session must not be reset even if the incoming session restarts. The Observation Domain ID of a Mediator need not describe Observation Points on the Mediator itself, so the Mediator should export the Original Exporter's IP address and Observation Domain ID, as far as privacy policy permits.
sections.eli5: The workers can stand in a row or side by side. Sending each customer's reports to their own office is just a sorting worker followed by a mailing worker.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5101 apply to Mediators, as do those of RFC 5655 for those that write or store IPFIX Files. A Mediator is by design a "man in the middle": TLS cannot tie the session from the Original Exporter to the session toward the Collector.

The RFC adds specific rules. A Mediator that receives data over TLS or DTLS must by default send its output over TLS or DTLS as well, so protection is not downgraded. It may export in cleartext only when requirements allow, for example when it removes all confidential information or bridges to a physically protected network. In the other direction, a Mediator must not "upgrade" trust by signing data that came from an unprotected, untrusted source, and should tell the Collector when original protection was missing. Finally, data from multiple sources must be kept separate unless the Mediator exists to combine it, as in spatial aggregation.
sections.eli5: If the reports came in a locked box, the middleman should send them on in a locked box too, and should not put a trusted stamp on reports that came from a stranger.

items.title: Conversion
items.text: Non-IPFIX into IPFIX, or one IPFIX transport into another.

items.title: Selection
items.text: Passes only records that match a value or range.

items.title: Aggregation
items.text: Merges records by shared keys (spatial) or over time (temporal).

items.title: Anonymization
items.text: Deletes or masks fields to protect identities.

items.title: Correlation
items.text: Derives new data, such as delay or bidirectional flows.
